newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeking deal on new rules for steel industry aid.
newsitem.headline: EU seeking deal on new rules for steel industry aid.

text.p: European Union industry ministers will try to bridge their differences on Thursday in a bid to reach a compromise on controversial new rules for state aid to the steel sector before time runs out.
They are under pressure to find a solution on the Commission's draft proposal for a new steel state aid code, SEC(96)284, as the current rules expire on December 31.

Discussions at the May 20 Industry Council showed that member states were clearly divided with especially Britain but also Denmark, the Netherlands and Sweden fearing that the proposed code would lead to a weakening of the state aid rules.
Diplomats say the rules on aid to the steel sector are now generally tougher than rules on support to other EU industries.
EU officials say there are still differences of opinion between member states on the issue but that the gap has narrowed and that there is a will to find a compromise.
A representative of the Irish presidency said he was "reasonably optimistic" ahead of the talks.
"There will be a long and tough discussion," another diplomat predicted, adding however that all countries wanted to have a new code.
Britain was seen as holding the key on the issue.
"If the UK shows movement, others will follow," one official said.
A decision on a new code would need unanimous support.

Among other things, the proposal is intended to put the steel industry, still covered by the European Coal and Steel Community Treaty, on the same footing as other sectors when it comes to research and environmental protection aid.

A further novelty in the proposal is to allow closure aid also for "partial closures", for example the shutting down of one of a group's plants as long as the company as a whole does not increase capacity for five years.
Another potential problem is a Greek request to reintroduce a provision allowing limited regional aid in favour of the steel industry in Greece.

Britain, for example, fears that governments could use less stringent provisions on environmental aid to subsidise the creation of production plants if they could justify it in terms of environmental improvement.
London is strongly sceptical of state aid in general. In the steel sector, it also fears that aid in other countries may hurt British Steel.

Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert and DGIV (the directorate-general for competition) have disputed the British view, arguing that the proposal as a whole would in fact make the aid rules stricter.
If industry ministers fail to agree, all cases of aid as from January 1 next year would have to be vetted by the Council, with all Commission decisions requiring the unanimous assent of ministers.
The new code would run until the year 2002 when the ECSC treaty expires but one EU diplomat said a special code would be needed for the sector even after that date.
Therefore, any code agreed now may also form the basis for rules lasting long after the expiry of the Treaty of Paris, he said.
